The Jazz Singer. A landmark film from 1927 directed by Alan Crosland and starring Al Jolson that introduced synchronized sound to mainstream American cinema. Though not the first sound film, it was the first feature-length narrative film with synchronized dialogue and singing. Its commercial success catalyzed the rapid conversion of Hollywood from silent to talking pictures, effectively ending the silent-film era within three years.

The Jazz Singer starred Al Jolson, a popular vaudeville and stage performer, as Jakie Rabinowitz, a Jewish cantor's son who dreams of becoming a popular singer. This created a narrative about assimilation and generational conflict that reflected real American anxieties. The film's Vitaphone system was a disc-based synchronized sound technology—a pre-recorded phonograph disc played in sync with the projected film. Primitive by later standards, it was revolutionary at the time.

Most of the film was still silent, with only a few scenes featuring synchronized dialogue and Jolson's singing. The bulk of exposition and plot remained conveyed through intertitles, reflecting the hybrid technology's limitations. Jolson's ad-libbed line, "Wait a minute, wait a minute, you ain't heard nothin' yet!", became cinema's symbolic first words, signaling the arrival of the speaking picture.

The film's release in October 1927 shocked the industry. Within eighteen months, the vast majority of American theaters had converted to sound equipment. By 1930, silent films were commercially extinct in the United States. Many acclaimed silent filmmakers resisted sound. Charlie Chaplin continued making silent films into the late 1930s. Others like D. W. Griffith saw their careers decline as they struggled with the new medium.

The transition was devastating for international cinema. Sound made films language-specific, reducing the global reach silent films had enjoyed. American dominance intensified as only major studios could afford rapid retooling.
